questions.explanation: Rearranging the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation gives a straight line of ln p against 1 over T whose slope is minus dHvap over R, so dHvap = -R times the slope. From the first two rows the slope is ln(0.0757/0.0300) divided by (1/300.0 - 1/325.0), which is 0.9256 over 0.00025641, or 3609.8, and multiplying by 8.314 gives 30012 J per mole, so 30.0 kJ per mole. The two adjacent pairs give 30.0 and 30.0 kJ per mole, which is the internal consistency check: a genuine vapour pressure table is very nearly a straight line in ln p against 1 over T, and agreement between overlapping pairs is the evidence that the constant enthalpy assumption holds over this range.

questions.explanation: Work done by the gas is the area under each leg. Along A to B the gas expands at 100 kPa from 1 to 3 cubic metres, so it does 100 x 2 = 200 J. Along B to C and along D to A the gas is compressed against rising and falling pressure, and along C to D it is compressed at 20 kPa, so it has 20 x 2 = 40 J done on it, and the two adiabats contribute equal and opposite amounts that cancel. The enclosed area is therefore 200 - 40 = 160 J, which is the net work of the cycle, and dividing by the 200 J absorbed at the hot isotherm gives the efficiency of 0.80, exactly the Carnot value 1 - 20/100 for these two pressure levels. The area under the lower isotherm alone, 40 J, is the work returned to the cold reservoir, not the output.
questions.hint: Take the area under each leg, add the legs where the gas expands and subtract the legs where it is compressed.

answer.exemplar: A good answer prepares a series of buffers at fixed total concentration of 0.050 mol per litre but varying ratio of A- to HA, for example 0.050 mol per litre of acid alone, then 0.025 with 0.025, then 0.010 with 0.040. It measures the pH of each with a calibrated glass electrode at a fixed temperature, converts each reading to a hydrogen ion concentration, and applies the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation rearranged as pKa = pH - log of the ratio of base to acid, so that the ratio is read from the quantities mixed rather than from the electrode. It then plots pH against the logarithm of the ratio: a straight line of slope one whose intercept is pKa, or computes pKa from each buffer separately and averages. The single assumption is that activities may be replaced by molar concentrations, that the electrode reads the activity rather than the concentration, and that the mixture does not change volume on mixing, so the ratio by moles equals the ratio by concentration. Using several ratios and checking that the fitted slope is one is the built-in test of that assumption; a slope noticeably below one indicates activity corrections matter. The answer must reject a procedure that infers the constant from a single pH reading of the acid alone without any extrapolation, since that only bounds Ka, and must note that the temperature must be held and reported because Ka depends on it.

questions.explanation: Each buffer's pH fixes the ratio, so plot pH against the logarithm of the mixed ratio and read the intercept as pKa.
questions.hint: Mix the acid and its conjugate base in several known ratios, and note which single assumption lets moles stand in for activities.

answer.exemplar: A good answer says that the apparent units in the quotient come from the ratio of stoichiometric coefficients raised to the power of the number of moles of change, so the powers of concentration never cancel completely unless the number of moles is zero. The resolution is that the activities, not the concentrations, are what the thermodynamic definition uses: an activity is a concentration divided by the standard state concentration, which makes it a pure number, and the standard state factors are what cancel the leftover units. The quantity actually held constant is the standard pressure or standard concentration, fixed by convention rather than by the reaction. A good answer also says that the numerical value of a constant is therefore conventional: a change of units, or a change of standard state, multiplies the number by a predictable power of the conversion factor, so the quoted constant is meaningless without its standard state. It should add that this is why a constant quoted without its units and standard state can be compared only with another quoted the same way, and that the common practice of attaching apparent units to a pressure-based constant is a convenience that hides a convention rather than a real dimensional fact.
